title: Stop Gaslighting Teachers
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Reading specialist Harriett Janetos argues that reading instruction should be organized around one agreed principle: students must decode new words so that orthographic mapping can store them for automatic recognition. Prompted by watching a second-grader decode three pronunciations of 'ea' in a story title, she contrasts the Linnea Ehri and David Share line of research with the Ken Goodman and Marie Clay cueing tradition. She walks through an eight-step cueing chart to show how it detours around decoding and calls the result instructional gaslighting of teachers who sense it is not helping. The piece mixes anecdote, humor and the history of the reading wars to press its point. It closes with a call for education professors to change coursework as the research dictates.
points: Decoding is the on-ramp to orthographic mapping, so foundational skills instruction should be judged by whether it helps students decode and store new words.
Linnea Ehri's decades of research against the Goodman 'guessing game' theory is offered as the model of how evidence should win over influential pet theories.
Walking the cueing chart step by step on a real title shows how many prompts a student must pass through before reaching the one that matters, trying different pronunciations.

Teachers told to doubt their own skepticism about approaches that leave children behind are being gaslit, and teacher-preparation faculty carry responsibility for updating courses as research changes.
quotes: Something snapped because I realized this was a perfect illustration of how senseless the circuitous route to reading instruction promoted by Whole Language and Balanced Literacy advocates can sometimes be (examples to follow). It can waste time, to be sure, but more importantly, it can crowd out more effective and efficient methods that might never gain purchase if they are not prioritized.
If we could just come together and agree on this one single thing—what readers do when they encounter new words and why they need to do it—it would make a big difference to our students.
Fifteen years working as a reading specialist with hundreds of struggling readers has made it clear to me that we have been subjected, and continue to be subjected, to instructional gaslighting.

Because we’ve lifted our eyes away from the word instead of keeping them laser-focused on it to help students use their own eyes to lift words off the page, we’ve failed to recognize what word recognition entails.

The goal isn’t just to get through the words on the page in any way possible and live to tell the tale. The goal is to get through the words and add those words to your lexicon so that the next encounter with them becomes that much easier.
This is what I mean by gaslighting: giving me stuff that doesn’t make sense and then daring me to deny it’s helpful.
Clinging to pet theories and passing them on to teachers with unwavering conviction displays an alarming level of hubris that harms children.
